title: Standard for the Transmission of IP Datagrams over IEEE 802 Networks
summary: Specifies a standard way to carry IP datagrams and ARP requests and replies over IEEE 802 networks, so that implementations are compatible and interoperable. It was an Internet standard and replaces RFC 948.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1042 defines how to place IP datagrams and ARP messages inside frames on IEEE 802 networks. A common header tells the receiving device whether the frame carries IP or an address-resolution message.

questions: how are ip datagrams sent over ieee 802
what is ip encapsulation on ieee 802 networks
what is the mtu for ieee 802.3 networks
how does arp map addresses on ieee 802
what is the 802.3 ip datagram size
subtitle: The agreed frame format for sending IP datagrams and ARP messages over IEEE 802 LANs.

tldr.problem: IEEE 802 LAN types use different frame rules, so hosts need a common way to carry IP datagrams and Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) messages on each network type.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC places IP and ARP inside an 802.2 LLC and SNAP header. The SNAP EtherType identifies IP or ARP, and ARP maps Internet addresses to IEEE 802 hardware addresses.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1042 specifies interoperable transmission rules for 802.3, 802.4 and 802.5 networks. It is an Internet Standard that obsoletes RFC 948.

today: RFC 1042 is an Internet Standard published in February 1988. It obsoletes RFC 948 and has no later updates listed in the work-unit metadata.

sections.title: Goal and Network Scope
sections.content:
The RFC aims to make implementations interoperate when sending IP datagrams and ARP requests and replies over IEEE 802 networks. It covers 802.3, 802.4 and 802.5. Implementations need to behave consistently within each network type; the document does not require identical use across all three.

IEEE 802.2 supplies the Logical Link Control (LLC) layer, while each network type has its own physical and Media Access Control rules. The RFC describes how IP and ARP fit over those layers.
sections.plainLanguage: Different IEEE 802 networks have different frame rules. This RFC gives hosts a shared method for carrying IP and ARP on each of the network types it covers.

sections.title: The LLC and SNAP Header
sections.content:
IP datagrams and ARP messages are carried inside 802.2 LLC and SNAP, over the network's MAC layer. The LLC and SNAP headers together use 8 octets. The fields identify SNAP and include an EtherType for the payload.

The RFC sets both service access point fields to 170, the LLC control field to 3 and the SNAP organization code to zero. The EtherType is 2048 for IP and 2054 for ARP. Type 1 communication must be supported by all implementations.
sections.plainLanguage: A short header sits in front of the IP or ARP data. Its EtherType tells the receiver which kind of message follows.

sections.title: Using ARP to Find a Hardware Address
sections.content:
A 32-bit Internet address must be mapped to a 16-bit or 48-bit IEEE 802 address using ARP. Each host knows its own Internet address, answers ARP requests and uses ARP to find the hardware address for another host.

For IEEE 802, the ARP hardware type is 6; the protocol type for IP is 2048. The hardware-address length is 2 or 6 octets, depending on the network address size, and the IP protocol-address length is 4 octets. ARP operation 1 is a request and operation 2 is a reply.
sections.plainLanguage: Before sending a frame, a host needs the destination's local hardware address. ARP asks which hardware address matches an Internet address and receives a reply.

sections.title: Frame Padding and Datagram Sizes
sections.content:
If a network requires a minimum frame size, the data may be padded with zero octets. That padding is not part of the IP datagram and is not included in its total-length field. All hosts on a particular network must use the same MTU.

The maximum IP datagram depends on the network's frame limit and MAC overhead. For example, the RFC gives 1492 octets for a 10BASE5 802.3 network, 8166 for 802.4 and 4464 for an 802.5 ring with a 9 millisecond token-holding time at 4 megabits per second. Hosts must not send datagrams longer than 576 octets unless they know the destination can accept them.
sections.plainLanguage: Each network has a maximum frame size, and the link headers take up some of that space. The remaining room determines how large an IP datagram can be.

sections.title: Source Routing on 802.5
sections.content:
Some 802.5 token-ring networks use a Routing Information Field (RIF) in the MAC header to carry a route across multiple rings. The source address indicates whether the RIF is present. The RIF includes routing-control information and route-designator fields.

For IP broadcasts, the RFC requires a single-route broadcast so receivers do not get multiple copies. ARP may first use an all-stations broadcast on the local ring and then, if needed, a broadcast that crosses rings. Implementations must understand frames with no RIF or an empty RIF.
sections.plainLanguage: A token-ring frame can include a route through connected rings. IP broadcasts use a single route so a destination does not receive duplicate copies.

sections.title: Coexisting with Ethernet and Trailers
sections.content:
Some systems may use trailer encapsulation with other systems that support it, but every host must still communicate using the standard non-trailer method. This keeps the standard format available when optional behavior is not shared.

Ethernet and IEEE 802.3 link protocols can share one physical cable, but link-level broadcasts reach only devices using the same link protocol. The RFC recommends treating them as two networks connected by an IP gateway. It also notes that Ethernet permits a 1500-octet IP datagram while the specified 802.3 format permits 1492 octets.
sections.plainLanguage: Optional trailer formats work only when both ends support them, so the standard format remains necessary. Ethernet and 802.3 broadcasts do not reach every device on a shared cable.
